title: The (Few but Purposeful) Classroom Posters I Use
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart walks through the small, deliberate set of posters he hangs in his classroom, arguing that posters are only multipliers of understanding a teacher already brings, decoration if unused, powerful signals if taught into and referenced regularly. He covers his Everest Statement, Do hard things, The bell is our boss, It's not personal, it's business, his five classroom management rules, the Knowledge x Practice x Time = Mastery equation, the Rainbow of Why, PVLEGS, and Pop-Up Debate Rules, each tied back to a specific belief or strategy from his broader framework rather than treated as generic classroom decor.
points: Stuart's core claim about posters is that they are not magical, they're physical signals that support the verbal and non-verbal signals a teacher already sends, meaning their value depends entirely on how deliberately they're taught and referenced.
It's not personal. It's business exists specifically to help students unpack outcomes without letting results damage their Efficacy or Belonging beliefs.
His five classroom management rules poster intentionally avoids vague language like respect, instead pairing each specific rule with a rationale he can invoke when addressing misbehavior.
The Knowledge x Practice x Time = Mastery poster distills a much longer book argument into a handful of words meant to show students that growing toward mastery is possible for anyone.
quotes: If I don't deeply understand what they mean and how to develop that understanding in the minds of my learners, they are mere decorations. But if I work hard to understand them and use them in my instruction, they become powerful signals of what we're after in my classroom.
This is where it all begins and ends for me. What, in a single sentence, is the work we do in my classroom all about?

This one's important for helping my students unpack outcomes, good or bad, without letting those outcomes undermine their Efficacy and Belonging beliefs. Taking assessment results personally is a huuuuuuuuuuge obstacle to student motivation.

In the past, I've experimented with leaving this rule out, instead teaching my students to monitor their own voices and be aware of the others in the room. I have found that this is not something I can reasonably expect 30+ adolescents to be proficient at.

What I'm trying to help them see, day after day, is that growing toward mastery is possible for anyone. All that it takes is building knowledge, practicing with that knowledge, and doing so day after day.
